"![](images/b5/b5b4d260ad31b6c4efc3f7314e98df8b422f8d92f0f21fa436334c4b15d88a67.png)\n\nConsider a sample of size $n=100$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Given that the proportion of those in the sample with the characteristic is $\\widehat{\\,p}=0.64$, find a $90\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of individuals having this characteristic.\n\n*Hint: Use the fact that $P(Z > 1.645) = 0.05$, where $Z \\sim N(0,1)$, as shown in the diagram above.*" :question/worked-solution "Since $n=100$ and\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p}=0.64\n$$\n\nwe have that\n\n- $n \\widehat{\\,p} = 100 \\cdot 0.64 = 64 > 5$, and\n- $n(1-\\widehat{\\,p}) = 100 \\cdot (1-0.64) = 36 > 5$.\n\nAs a result, we may use the following normal approximation:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p} - p}{\\sqrt{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})/n}\\phantom{\\mid}} \\sim N(0,1)\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $\\!\\widehat{\\,p}$ is the sample proportion,\n- $p$ is the population proportion, and\n- $n$ is the sample size.\n\nGiven a value $\\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\\alpha)]\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\pm z_{\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}}\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n$$\nP(Z > z_{\\alpha/2}) = \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nand $Z \\sim N(0,1)$.\n\nWe are interested in finding a $90\\%$ confidence interval. So, we have\n\n$$\n\\alpha=1-0.9=0.1 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}=0.05\n$$\n\nWe are given that\n\n$$\nP(Z > 1.645) = 0.05\n$$\n\nAs a result,\n\n$$\nz_{\\alpha/2} = z_{0.05} = 1.645\n$$\n\nTherefore, a $90\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:\n\n$$\n0.64 ± 1.645 \\cdot \\sqrt{(0.64(1 - 0.64))/(100)}; 0.64 ± 0.079\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186049862} {:db/id 17592186050921} {:db/id 17592186172323 :question/id #uuid "d4c85404-18e8-5990-bb12-ba8d0d33ef92" :question/math-academy-id "q-142713"} {:db/id 17592186172324 :question/id #uuid "9b09786c-003f-565a-9fd2-fe6264490f01" :question/math-academy-id "q-142715" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186171935 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "02674ca9-e650-5dc8-93a5-893040bf5342" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals for Population Proportions"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "820a5f1b-40bc-5b51-83cd-74e72b152309" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.65 ± 0.201" :db/id 17592186168808} {:answer/id #uuid "8c574c8c-ffcb-596a-86f7-2c17a7ec1049" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.65 ± 0.093" :db/id 17592186168809} {:answer/id #uuid "b5830626-811c-5f31-a770-d36a4e7e6cf3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.65 ± 0.052" :db/id 17592186168810} {:answer/id #uuid "dba92f05-9a2c-5c93-b1fc-5b35b844653b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.95 ± 0.012" :db/id 17592186168811} {:answer/id #uuid "587cec6c-a924-59ad-87aa-15967c86eaef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.95 ± 0.132" :db/id 17592186168812}] :answer-field/id #uuid "fb8692a1-74f0-5ff4-a1e6-f0adf87799e3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186168807}] :question/problem "Consider a sample of size $n = 100$ from a large population where some individuals have a particular characteristic. Find a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all U.S. households that own at least one dog.\n\n*Hint: Given a random variable $Z \\sim N(0,1)$, the table below shows the $z$-scores $z_p$ such that $P(Z > z_p) = p$ for some particular values of $p$.*\n\n| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $0.025$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $z_p$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $1.960$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |" :question/worked-solution "First, let's interpret the data:\n\n- the population consists of all U.S. households,\n- some of the households surveyed own at least one dog, and some don't,\n- the size of the random sample is $n=1\\, 500$, and\n- the proportion of households in the sample that own at least one dog can be found as follows:\n\n$$\n\\widehat{p\\,} = \\dfrac{780}{1\\, 500} = 0.52\n$$\n\nNow, we have that\n\n- $n \\widehat{\\,p} =1\\,500 \\cdot 0.52 = 780 > 5$, and\n- $n(1-\\widehat{\\,p}) = 1\\,500 \\cdot (1-0.52) = 720 > 5$.\n\nAs a result, we may use the following normal approximation:\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p} - p}{\\sqrt{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})/n}\\phantom{\\mid}} \\sim N(0,1)\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $\\!\\widehat{\\,p}$ is the sample proportion,\n- $p$ is the population proportion, and\n- $n$ is the sample size.\n\nGiven a value $\\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, the corresponding $[100(1-\\alpha)]\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ of the original distribution can be written as\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\pm z_{\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}}\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n$$\nP(Z > z_{\\alpha/2}) = \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nand $Z \\sim N(0,1)$.\n\nWe are interested in finding a $95\\%$ confidence interval. So, we have\n\n$$\n\\alpha=1-0.95=0.05 \\qquad\\Longrightarrow\\qquad \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}=0.025\n$$\n\nWe also need to find the $z$-score value $z_{0.025}$ such that\n\n$$\nP(Z > z_{0.025}) = 0.025\n$$\n\nwhere $Z \\sim N(0,1)$.\n\n![](images/f5/f58f278f66244732c379f3ad0f064227298915b8e7c364b91b8766bb8789c1ea.png)\n\nFrom the percentage points table of the normal distribution, we obtain that\n\n$$\nz_{0.025}=1.96{:}\n$$\n\n| $p$ | $0.100$ | $0.050$ | $\\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\\color{blue}0.025}$ | $0.010$ | $0.005$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $z_p$ | $1.282$ | $1.645$ | $\\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\\color{blue}1.960}$ | $2.326$ | $2.576$ |\n\nTherefore, a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is the following:\n\n$$\n0.52 ± 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(0.52(1 - 0.52))/(1500)}; 0.52 ± 0.025\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186172325 :question/id #uuid "42e7a19f-f4f3-5e6a-9979-741a2870cc54" :question/math-academy-id "q-142726" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186171936 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f2b987ad-6854-59a6-bb39-c7f3c0a3db75" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Confidence Intervals for Population Proportions In Context"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a30fb77f-030b-5fb5-8599-5389e13855b1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.24 ± 0.091" :db/id 17592186168814} {:answer/id #uuid "a4c5a202-7c9e-5f90-adcd-0a0668db6b98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.16 ± 0.005" :db/id 17592186168815} {:answer/id #uuid "d6619d48-23d6-5b2d-80eb-23a38f4b6727" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.16 ± 0.017" :db/id 17592186168816} {:answer/id #uuid "010d656e-d5e9-54b5-b49a-26e305a6c30a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.24 ± 0.028" :db/id 17592186168817} {:answer/id #uuid "2aa7d13f-058c-5005-a0a5-efe46c7aae4e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.16 ± 0.059" :db/id 17592186168818}] :answer-field/id #uuid "8362fec0-95c3-51e3-8cbd-6c9d9645d33c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186168813}] :question/problem "A survey of $150$ randomly selected students at a particular university showed that only $24$ select at least one math course. :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186172722 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173212 :tutorial/content "Let's now discuss how to construct a confidence interval for the proportion of the population whose members have a particular characteristic.\n\nAs a concrete example, let $p$ represent the proportion of the United States voting population that will vote for candidate $A$ in the next presidential election.\n\nSuppose we conduct a random sample of size $n=40$ from our population. After processing our results, we find that the proportion $\\widehat{\\,p}$ of sample members that plan to vote for candidate $A$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} = 0.3\n$$\n\nThis is our *estimate* of the population proportion $p$.\n\nOf course, the quantity that we're *really* interested in is $p$, the proportion of the entire voting population that will vote for candidate $A$. We want to get an idea of how accurate our estimate is. Therefore, we wish to construct a confidence interval of the form\n\n$$\n(\\widehat{\\,p}-E, \\: \\widehat{\\,p}+E)\n$$\n\nwhere $E$ is some **margin of error.**\n\nLet's now discuss how to construct a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$." :tutorial/id #uuid "b64af41f-7266-5dc3-9360-aa6c591384e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6254 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "89f797af-a45c-58a5-8bec-5490a8e51df2" :step/math-academy-id 176376 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172723}} {:db/id 17592186172723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173223 :tutorial/content "We have\n\n$$\nn=40, \\widehat{\\,p} = 0.3\n$$\n\nand we wish to construct a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$.\n\nTo construct our confidence interval, the first thing to do is to establish the sampling distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$.\n\nSince the United States has around $240$ million registered voters, the sample size $n=40$ is clearly less than $10\\%$ of the population size. This means that, provided certain conditions are met, the following approximation can be applied:\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\sim N\\left(p, \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \\right)\n$$\n\nLet's check that our usual conditions hold in this case (where we use $\\widehat{\\,p}$ as an estimate for $p$):\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nnp^(^) &= 40 \\cdot 0.3 \\\\\n&= 12 \\\\\n&> 5✓ \\\\\nn(1 - p^(^)) &= 40 \\cdot (1 - 0.3) \\\\\n&= 28 \\\\\n&> 5✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince all three conditions hold, the above approximation is applicable.\n\nBy transforming $\\widehat{\\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have\n\n$$\nZ= \\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p} - p}{\\sqrt{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})/n}\\phantom{\\mid}} \\sim N(0,1)\n$$\n\nWe wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:\n\n![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)\n\nTo help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\\alpha$. Since we're computing a $95\\%$ confidence interval, we have\n\n$$\n\\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}=0.025\n$$\n\nNotice that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nis precisely the area bounded by each \"tail\" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\\pm z_{\\alpha/2}$:\n\n![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)\n\nAccording to our diagram,\n\n$$\nP(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025\n$$\n\nUsing a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that\n\n$$\nz_{0.025} \\approx 1.96\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025\n$$\n\nIn other words,\n\n$$\nP(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95\n$$\n\nTherefore, there is a $95\\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96)$.\n\nNow, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population proportion $p$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}-1.96 & < Z < 1.96 \\\\ -1.96 & < (p^(^) - p)/(\\sqrt{p^(^)(1 - p^(^))/n}) < 1.96 \\\\ -1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & < p^(^) - p < 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} \\\\ -p^(^) - 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & < - p < - p^(^) + 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} \\\\ p^(^) + 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & > p > p^(^) - 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} \\\\ p^(^) - 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & < p < p^(^) + 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)}\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nTherefore, a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion ${p}$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\left(\\widehat{\\,p} -1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}},\\: \\widehat{\\,p} +1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}} \\right)\n$$\n\nFinally, substituting our values\n\n$$\nn=40, \\qquad \\widehat{\\,p}=0.3\n$$\n\nwe obtain that our $95\\%$ confidence interval for ${p}$ is\n\n$$\n\\big(0.3 - 0.142, \\: 0.3 + 0.142 \\big)\n$$\n\nwhich simplifies to\n\n$$\n\\big(0.158, \\: 0.442 \\big)\n$$\n\nNow that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "462ecbef-51e0-5a01-808e-cd71bd17cbc2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6462 :tutorial/title "Constructing Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "413a1302-d708-5a68-8969-eee6f8bf3793" :step/math-academy-id 176377 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172724}} {:db/id 17592186172724 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173213 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a random sample of size $n$ from a sufficiently large population with sample proportion $\\widehat{\\,p}$. Let's also assume that the following conditions are satisfied:\n\n- $n \\widehat{\\,p} > 5$\n- $n (1-\\widehat{\\,p}) > 5$\n\nThen, for a given value $\\alpha$ between $0$ and $1$, a $[100(1-\\alpha)]\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\left(\\widehat{\\,p} - z_{\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}},\\: \\widehat{\\,p} + z_{\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}} \\right)\n$$\n\nThe endpoints of our confidence interval are the **confidence limits** and are given by\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\pm z_{\\alpha/2} \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}}\n$$\n\nEach part of the formula above has a name:\n\n- $\\!\\widehat{\\,p}$ is the sample proportion\n- $p$ is the population proportion\n- $n$ is the sample size\n- $z_{\\alpha/2}$ is the corresponding $z$-score\n- $E = z_{\\alpha/2}\\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}}$ is the margin of error\n\n$$\nz\n$$\n\nSo, our confidence interval can be written as follows:\n\n$$\n(p^(^) - [margin of error],\\begin{vmatrix}p^(^) + [margin of error]) \\\\ (p^(^) - [[math]z[/math]-score] \\cdot [standard error], \\mid p^(^) + [[math]z[/math]-score] \\cdot [standard error]) \\\\ (p^(^) - z_{α/2} \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)},\\end{vmatrix}p^(^) + z_{α/2} \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)})\n$$\n\nSince computing a confidence interval amounts to finding the corresponding confidence limits, we will use the two terms interchangeably.\n\nFinally, in the future, you may assume that if a population is \"large,\" it is sufficiently larger than any sample drawn from it." :tutorial/id Therefore, we wish to construct a confidence interval of the form\n\n$$\n(\\widehat{\\,p}-E, \\: \\widehat{\\,p}+E)\n$$\n\nwhere $E$ is some **margin of error.**\n\nLet's now discuss how to construct a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$." :tutorial/id #uuid "b64af41f-7266-5dc3-9360-aa6c591384e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6254 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "89f797af-a45c-58a5-8bec-5490a8e51df2" :step/math-academy-id 176376 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172723}} {:db/id 17592186173212 :tutorial/content "Let's now discuss how to construct a confidence interval for the proportion of the population whose members have a particular characteristic.\n\nAs a concrete example, let $p$ represent the proportion of the United States voting population that will vote for candidate $A$ in the next presidential election.\n\nSuppose we conduct a random sample of size $n=40$ from our population. After processing our results, we find that the proportion $\\widehat{\\,p}$ of sample members that plan to vote for candidate $A$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} = 0.3\n$$\n\nThis is our *estimate* of the population proportion $p$.\n\nOf course, the quantity that we're *really* interested in is $p$, the proportion of the entire voting population that will vote for candidate $A$. We want to get an idea of how accurate our estimate is. Therefore, we wish to construct a confidence interval of the form\n\n$$\n(\\widehat{\\,p}-E, \\: \\widehat{\\,p}+E)\n$$\n\nwhere $E$ is some **margin of error.**\n\nLet's now discuss how to construct a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$." :tutorial/id #uuid "b64af41f-7266-5dc3-9360-aa6c591384e4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6254 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186172723 :step/content {:db/id 17592186173223 :tutorial/content "We have\n\n$$\nn=40, \\widehat{\\,p} = 0.3\n$$\n\nand we wish to construct a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$.\n\nTo construct our confidence interval, the first thing to do is to establish the sampling distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$.\n\nSince the United States has around $240$ million registered voters, the sample size $n=40$ is clearly less than $10\\%$ of the population size. This means that, provided certain conditions are met, the following approximation can be applied:\n\n$$\n\\widehat{\\,p} \\sim N\\left(p, \\dfrac{p(1-p)}{n} \\right)\n$$\n\nLet's check that our usual conditions hold in this case (where we use $\\widehat{\\,p}$ as an estimate for $p$):\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nnp^(^) &= 40 \\cdot 0.3 \\\\\n&= 12 \\\\\n&> 5✓ \\\\\nn(1 - p^(^)) &= 40 \\cdot (1 - 0.3) \\\\\n&= 28 \\\\\n&> 5✓\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince all three conditions hold, the above approximation is applicable.\n\nBy transforming $\\widehat{\\,p}$ to a standard normal random variable, we have\n\n$$\nZ= \\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p} - p}{\\sqrt{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})/n}\\phantom{\\mid}} \\sim N(0,1)\n$$\n\nWe wish to find a $z$-interval that we're $95\\%$ confident that the random variable $Z$ lies within. This interval is indicated in the diagram below:\n\n![](images/50/50a0f49fe5c96ba3259832fbf1a0abcedffb342301ca069bb7b88d157a181019.png)\n\nTo help with the notation, we define a new parameter $\\alpha$. Since we're computing a $95\\%$ confidence interval, we have\n\n$$\n\\alpha=1-0.95=0.05\\quad\\Longrightarrow\\quad \\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}=0.025\n$$\n\nNotice that\n\n$$\n\\dfrac{\\alpha}{2}\n$$\n\nis precisely the area bounded by each \"tail\" that we're excluding from our confidence interval. Let's label the critical values at the endpoints of our interval as $\\pm z_{\\alpha/2}$:\n\n![](images/3c/3cdfd2c72bf7fe65e5d1b584d46d4c846e74615e54c739a6d1ea990c95011a8a.png)\n\nAccording to our diagram,\n\n$$\nP(Z > z_{0.025}) = P(Z < -z_{0.025}) = 0.025\n$$\n\nUsing a percentage points table for the standard normal distribution, we find that\n\n$$\nz_{0.025} \\approx 1.96\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nP(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025\n$$\n\nIn other words,\n\n$$\nP(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95\n$$\n\nTherefore, there is a $95\\%$ probability that our random variable $Z$ will lie in the interval $(-1.96, 1.96)$.\n\nNow, here's the trick. We solve the inequality inside the parentheses of the last probability statement for the population proportion $p$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{bmatrix}-1.96 & < Z < 1.96 \\\\ -1.96 & < (p^(^) - p)/(\\sqrt{p^(^)(1 - p^(^))/n}) < 1.96 \\\\ -1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & < p^(^) - p < 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} \\\\ -p^(^) - 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & < - p < - p^(^) + 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} \\\\ p^(^) + 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & > p > p^(^) - 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} \\\\ p^(^) - 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & < p < p^(^) + 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)}\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nTherefore, a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion ${p}$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\left(\\widehat{\\,p} -1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}},\\: \\widehat{\\,p} +1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{\\dfrac{\\widehat{\\,p}(1-\\widehat{\\,p})}{n}} \\right)\n$$\n\nFinally, substituting our values\n\n$$\nn=40, \\qquad \\widehat{\\,p}=0.3\n$$\n\nwe obtain that our $95\\%$ confidence interval for ${p}$ is\n\n$$\n\\big(0.3 - 0.142, \\: 0.3 + 0.142 \\big)\n$$\n\nwhich simplifies to\n\n$$\n\\big(0.158, \\: 0.442 \\big)\n$$\n\nNow that we've seen how to construct a particular confidence interval, let's discuss the more general procedure." :tutorial/id #uuid "462ecbef-51e0-5a01-808e-cd71bd17cbc2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6462 :tutorial/title "Constructing Confidence Intervals"} :step/id #uuid "413a1302-d708-5a68-8969-eee6f8bf3793" :step/math-academy-id 176377 :step/next {:db/id 17592186172724}} {:db/id 17592186173223 :tutorial/content "We have\n\n$$\nn=40, \\widehat{\\,p} = 0.3\n$$\n\nand we wish to construct a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion $p$.\n\nTo construct our confidence interval, the first thing to do is to establish the sampling distribution of $\\widehat{\\,p}$.\n\nSince the United States has around $240$ million registered voters, the sample size $n=40$ is clearly less than $10\\%$ of the population size. Find $f(0)$ if ${f(2)=3}$.\n\n![](images/87/8712bb0e61664a6d2ce86b465de2ff5c2d87fd159aa120e5eb6cae633585fbb8.png)" :question/worked-solution "The fundamental theorem of calculus states that\n\n$$\n\\int_{0}^{2} f'(x) \\: \\textrm{d}x = f(2) - f(0)\n$$\n\nand we know that\n\n$$\nf(2)=3\n$$\n\nso we can find $f(0)$ if we can figure out the value of the integral.\n\nRemember that the integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis. To compute the area under the curve, let's split up the integral into two integrals which represent areas that are easier to compute:\n\n$$\n\\int_{0}^{2} f'(x)\\: \\textrm{d}x = \\underbrace{\\int_{0}^{1} f'(x)\\: \\textrm{d}x}_{A_1} + \\underbrace{\\int_{1}^{2} f'(x)\\: \\textrm{d}x}_{A_2}\n$$\n\nThe $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \\in [0,1]$. The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nA_{1} &= \\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h \\\\\n&= \\frac{1}{2} \\cdot (1 + 2) \\cdot 1 \\\\\n&= \\frac{3}{2}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x \\in [1,2]$. The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nA_{2} &= \\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h \\\\\n&= \\frac{1}{2} \\cdot (1 + 2) \\cdot 1 \\\\\n&= \\frac{3}{2}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSo, the value of the original integral is\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\int_{0}^{2}f^{′}(x)dx &= A_{1} + A_{2} \\\\\n&= \\frac{3}{2} + \\frac{3}{2} \\\\\n&= 3\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, using the value above and the fact that\n\n$$\nf(2)=3\n$$\n\nwe get\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n3 &= f(2) - f(0) \\\\\n3 &= 3 - f(0) \\\\\nf(0) &= 0\n\\end{aligned}\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186101294 :question/id #uuid "63abac52-da08-5850-9b63-f4c73a2e093d" :question/math-academy-id "q-19600"} {:db/id 17592186101295 :question/id #uuid "76a38425-e321-502d-92cd-afc27c375a32" :question/math-academy-id "q-19602"} {:db/id 17592186100853 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100679 :question/id #uuid "20da9010-55f7-5e44-ba73-1c881084e4b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-431"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "64725151-b0e8-55f8-b910-358d4d2b1d36" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048227} {:db/id 17592186050057}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101268 :question/id #uuid "61e95e97-d183-5cb2-810d-a74a265d1b66" :question/math-academy-id "q-18066"} {:db/id 17592186101544 :question/id #uuid "f6efa7e3-8be8-56a3-a68d-9e8131a012bc" :question/math-academy-id "q-83002"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of a Function Given a Graph With Labeled Areas"} {:db/id 17592186100679 :question/id #uuid "20da9010-55f7-5e44-ba73-1c881084e4b2" :question/math-academy-id "e-431" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186100853 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "64725151-b0e8-55f8-b910-358d4d2b1d36" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Value of a Function Given a Graph With Labeled Areas"}] :question/problem "The function $f(x)$ is defined and differentiable on the interval $[-1,5]$. The algorithm for computing an SVD of a rectangular $m\\times n$ matrix $(m\\neq n)$ is similar to the algorithm for square matrices.\n\nAs an example, let's consider the matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/f6/f65e0eee905da85ce0be4bbf39546c2b31c2bac082ff00a6a1d54fd5b89a4a4e.svg)\n\nNotice that $A$ is a ${\\color{blue}{3}}\\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix. So, to compute the SVD of $A,$ we must write\n\n$$\nA=U \\Sigma V^T,\n$$\n\nwhere\n\n- $\\Sigma$ is a ${\\color{blue}{3}}\\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix with the singular values of $A$ (ordered from largest to smallest) on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,\n\n- $U$ is an orthogonal ${\\color{blue}{3}} \\times {\\color{blue}{3}}$ matrix,\n\n- $V$ is an orthogonal ${\\color{red}{2}} \\times {\\color{red}{2}}$ matrix.\n\nWe proceed as follows:\n\n- **Step 1.** Compute $A^T \\! A\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\\,A & ={[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.**  Find the singular values of $A.$ Computing the eigenvalues of $A^TA,$ we get\n\n$$\n\\lambda_1 = 4, \\qquad \\lambda_2 = 2.\n$$\n\nTherefore, the singular values of $A$ are \n\n$$\n\\sigma_1 = \\sqrt{\\lambda_1} =  2,  \\qquad \\sigma_2 = \\sqrt{\\lambda_2} =  \\sqrt{2}.\n$$\n\n- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of $A^T A$). Seeking non-zero solutions of $(A^T \\! A - \\lambda_1 I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ and $(A^T \\! A - \\lambda_2 I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvectors \n![](images/07/07085f021218ff17060b3c1a9099e1cabad24b3d12269f97f1fe50d49b970f6b.svg)\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A.$ Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the first two columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\mathbf u_1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute $\\mathbf u_2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- The matrix $U$ is a $3\\times 3$ matrix. However, we do not have the third singular value, so we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \n![](images/71/71f89dbcee33bce284b3085b872fdb9da2cc41166fe8a0bd26ef0bb5fe6876aa.svg) \nsuch that \n![](images/9e/9edc744372650e86c27f31ef15ac575cc8203803bdc5fe5730390727fd37146a.svg)\nSolving this system, we get the following nonzero normalized solution:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\\Sigma,$ and $V\\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c2/c2bbd771d886da6b3a369b7e03345d1be75c18c26c66590598581d2d99590524.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "670f2f0c-5dc5-54ae-9a39-2166ee2414fd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4893 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find an SVD for the $2\\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/32/325fa7080fdd5f7fc5723a2304aac049a938dfd1b490f09a7a2ceabb0b934db8.svg)\n\nDirectly applying the standard approach to $A$ could be problematic because it requires finding the eigenvalues of the $4\\times 4$ matrix $A^T \\! A.$ \n\nIn such cases, it's usually more convenient to find an SVD of the transposed matrix $A^T$ and then take the transpose of the resulting SVD. In this case, we would only have to find the eigenvalues of a $2 \\times 2$ matrix.\n\nFor example, if\n\n$$\nA^T = U \\Sigma V^T\n$$\n\nis an SVD for $A^T,$ then\n\n$$\nA= \\left(A^T\\right)^T= \\left(U \\Sigma V^T\\right)^T=V\\Sigma^T U^T\n$$\n\nis an SVD for $A.$  \n\nGoing through our usual process, we find that an SVD for $A^T$ is\n\n![](images/78/7802bcf50374a71efc4c0a7754c5628e88e7f1dfac345bc9e590cfcebd89d8d1.svg)\n\nTaking the transpose of the above equation. we find that an SVD for $A$ :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.\n\nThis happens, for example, when:\n\n- an eigenvalue is repeated, or\n\n- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.\n\nIn these cases, we proceed as follows:\n\n- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  \n\nFor example, we solve an equation of the form\n\n$$\n(A^T A - \\lambda I)\\mathbf{v} = \\mathbf{0},\n$$\n\nor, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{u}_1 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0, \\qquad \\mathbf{u}_2 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0.\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  \n\nThis shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{v} = x\\,\\mathbf{b}_1 + y\\,\\mathbf{b}_2,\n$$\n\nwhere $x$ and $y$ are free variables.\n\n- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  \n\nWe usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.\n\n- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  \n\nIf the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.\n\n- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  \n\nAfter that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.\n\nThese unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$\n\n**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:\n\n- belong to the correct solution space,\n\n- are mutually orthogonal, and\n\n- have norm $1.$\n\nLet's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} :step/id #uuid "7dc02cbe-4a5d-5f2d-8ad3-baa5e8278916" :step/math-academy-id 648305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162946}}] :activity/title "Singular Value Decomposition of Larger Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162227} {:db/id 17592186162858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163233 :tutorial/content "We can compute a singular value decomposition (SVD) of any matrix! A - \\lambda_2 I)\\mathbf{v}=\\mathbf{0}$ gives the unit eigenvectors \n![](images/07/07085f021218ff17060b3c1a9099e1cabad24b3d12269f97f1fe50d49b970f6b.svg)\n\n- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A.$ Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the first two columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute $\\mathbf u_1\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute $\\mathbf u_2\\mathbin{:}$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ -1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- The matrix $U$ is a $3\\times 3$ matrix. However, we do not have the third singular value, so we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \n![](images/71/71f89dbcee33bce284b3085b872fdb9da2cc41166fe8a0bd26ef0bb5fe6876aa.svg) \nsuch that \n![](images/9e/9edc744372650e86c27f31ef15ac575cc8203803bdc5fe5730390727fd37146a.svg)\nSolving this system, we get the following nonzero normalized solution:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{3} & =[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrices $U,$ $\\Sigma,$ and $V\\mathbin{:}$\n\n![](images/c2/c2bbd771d886da6b3a369b7e03345d1be75c18c26c66590598581d2d99590524.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "670f2f0c-5dc5-54ae-9a39-2166ee2414fd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4893 648301 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162948}} {:db/id 17592186385970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186385971 :tutorial/content "In some singular value decomposition problems, we do not get all of the needed vectors from the usual formulas right away.\n\nThis happens, for example, when:\n\n- an eigenvalue is repeated, or\n\n- a singular value is zero, so the corresponding vector is not determined uniquely.\n\nIn these cases, we proceed as follows:\n\n- **Step 1.** Solve the system that defines the eigenspace (or orthogonal complement).  \n\nFor example, we solve an equation of the form\n\n$$\n(A^T A - \\lambda I)\\mathbf{v} = \\mathbf{0},\n$$\n\nor, when finding missing columns of $U,$ we solve orthogonality conditions such as\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{u}_1 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0, \\qquad \\mathbf{u}_2 \\cdot \\mathbf{u} = 0.\n$$\n\n- **Step 2.** Write the general solution using free variables.  \n\nThis shows that there are infinitely many solutions. For example, the solution might look like\n\n$$\n\\mathbf{v} = x\\,\\mathbf{b}_1 + y\\,\\mathbf{b}_2,\n$$\n\nwhere $x$ and $y$ are free variables.\n\n- **Step 3.** Choose convenient vectors from the solution space.  \n\nWe usually choose simple values for the free variables to get easy vectors. These vectors should be linearly independent and, if possible, already orthogonal.\n\n- **Step 4.** Orthogonalize the chosen vectors if necessary.  \n\nIf the vectors are not mutually orthogonal, we apply the Gram–Schmidt process.\n\n- **Step 5.** Normalize the vectors.  \n\nAfter that, we divide each vector by its norm to obtain unit vectors.\n\nThese unit vectors form an orthonormal basis for the solution space, and they can be used as the needed columns of $V$ or $U.$\n\n**Note:** In these situations, there is usually *more than one correct answer*. Different choices of free variables can produce different orthonormal bases, so the resulting SVD is not necessarily unique. What matters is that the chosen vectors:\n\n- belong to the correct solution space,\n\n- are mutually orthogonal, and\n\n- have norm $1.$\n\nLet's see a concrete example." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e93068a-566a-5c34-a459-3250d8a847d3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15621 :tutorial/title "Choosing Eigenvectors When Eigenvalues Repeat or Are Missing"} :step/id #uuid "7dc02cbe-4a5d-5f2d-8ad3-baa5e8278916" :step/math-academy-id 648305 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162946}} {:db/id 17592186162948 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163258 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find an SVD for the $2\\times 4$ matrix $A,$ given by\n\n![](images/32/325fa7080fdd5f7fc5723a2304aac049a938dfd1b490f09a7a2ceabb0b934db8.svg)\n\nDirectly applying the standard approach to $A$ could be problematic because it requires finding the eigenvalues of the $4\\times 4$ matrix $A^T \\! Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then\n\n- $Σ$ is a $3\\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,\n\n- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\\times 3$ matrix,\n\n- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nFrom the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\\sigma }_{2}=2.$\nAlso, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$\n\nTherefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\\\ 2 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ \\frac{6}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\\\ 2 & 2 \\\\ 1 & -2\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{4}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} \\\\ -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \n\n$$\n{u}_{3}=[\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{3}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nsuch that \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\\\ {u}_{2}\\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\\end{aligned}\\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.\n$$\n\nSolving this system, which is equivalent to\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0 \\\\ -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}}{x}_{2}-\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}}{x}_{3}=0\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\{\\begin{aligned}2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\\\ -{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwe get the nonzero normalized solution \n\n$$\n{u}_{3}=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 0 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrix $U:$\n\n$$\nU=[\\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\\\ \\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} & -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} & 0 \\\\ -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{5}} & -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{5}} & 0\\end{aligned}]\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "6ec7950f-72d8-5bef-a77f-3f5e2a3e06a0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186430364}} {:db/id \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nConsider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then\n\n- $Σ$ is a $3\\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,\n\n- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\\times 3$ matrix,\n\n- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nFrom the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\\sigma }_{1}=3$ and ${\\sigma }_{2}=1.$\nAlso, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$\n\nTherefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ -2 & -2 \\\\ -1 & 0\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{3}[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ -\\frac{4}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{3\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ -\\frac{4}{3\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ -\\frac{1}{3\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{1}[\\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\\\ -2 & -2 \\\\ -1 & 0\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \n\n$$\n{u}_{3}=[\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{3}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nsuch that \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\\\ {u}_{2}\\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\\end{aligned}\\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.\n$$\n\nSolving this system, which is equivalent to\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{3\\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\\frac{4}{3\\sqrt{2}}{x}_{2}-\\frac{1}{3\\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}+\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\\\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwe get the nonzero normalized solution \n\n$$\n{u}_{3}=[\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{2}{3} \\\\ -\\frac{1}{3} \\\\ \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrix $U:$\n\n$$\nU=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{3\\sqrt{2}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} & -\\frac{2}{3} \\\\ -\\frac{4}{3\\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\\frac{1}{3} \\\\ -\\frac{1}{3\\sqrt{2}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} & \\frac{2}{3}\\end{aligned}]\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "46bb3e49-3990-5b69-ab08-fafc145eef1c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186443411}} {:db/id 17592186443410 :step/content {:db/id 17592186443407 \\\\ 0 & 2 \\\\ 0 & 0\\end{aligned}],\\,V=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} & -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nConsider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the $3$rd column of the matrix $U?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that if  $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of a $3\\times 2$ matrix $A,$ then\n\n- $Σ$ is a $3\\times 2$ matrix with nonnegative elements on the main diagonal and zeroes outside the main diagonal,\n\n- $U$ is an orthogonal $3\\times 3$ matrix,\n\n- $V$ is an orthogonal $2\\times 2$ matrix.\n\nFrom the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\\sigma }_{1}=2\\sqrt{6}$ and ${\\sigma }_{2}=2.$\nAlso, the columns ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ of $V$ give us the right singular vectors of $A.$\n\nTherefore, we can compute the $1$st and $2$nd columns of $U$ as follows:\n\n- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2\\sqrt{6}}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\\\ 2 & 2 \\\\ 3 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2\\sqrt{6}}[\\begin{aligned}2\\sqrt{2} \\\\ 2\\sqrt{2} \\\\ 2\\sqrt{2}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\\frac{1}{{\\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\\\ 2 & 2 \\\\ 3 & 1\\end{aligned}][\\begin{aligned}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}\\sqrt{2} \\\\ 0 \\\\ -\\sqrt{2}\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} \\\\ 0 \\\\ -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nSince we do not have the third singular value, we can't use the same formula to find the third column of $U.$ But we know that $U$ must be orthogonal. Hence, we must find a vector \n\n$$\n{u}_{3}=[\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\\\ {x}_{2} \\\\ {x}_{3}\\end{aligned}]\n$$\n\nsuch that \n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\\\ {u}_{2}\\cdot {u}_{3}=0,\\end{aligned}\\,‖{u}_{3}‖=1.\n$$\n\nSolving this system, which is equivalent to\n\n$$\n\\{\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}{x}_{1}+\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}{x}_{2}+\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}}{x}_{3}=0 \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0\\end{aligned}\\,⟹\\,\\{\\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\\\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{3}=0,\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nwe get the nonzero normalized solution \n\n$$\n{u}_{3}=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{6}} \\\\ -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{6}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{6}}\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\nFinally, we construct the matrix $U:$\n\n$$\nU=[\\begin{aligned}\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{6}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}} & 0 & -\\frac{2}{\\sqrt{6}} \\\\ \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{3}} & -\\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}} & \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{6}}\\end{aligned}]\n$$"} :step/id #uuid "07212635-5697-56eb-b073-186df2f19fe5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500455}} {:db/id 17592186500396 :step/content {:db/id :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the acute angle between the vector $x$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}},$ where\n\n$$\n{a}_{1}=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}],\\,{a}_{2}=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}],\\,x=[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}].\n$$" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by\n\n$$\n{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x=A({A}^{T}\\,A)^{-1}\\,{A}^{T}\\,x.\n$$\n\nIn our case, we have\n\n$$\nA=[\\begin{aligned}| & | \\\\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\\\ | & |\\end{aligned}]=[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\,⟹\\,{A}^{T}=[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 & -1\\end{aligned}].\n$$\n\nTherefore, we get the following projection:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot {([\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot {[\\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 3\\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{8}[\\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\\\ -1 & 3\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ 0\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & 1 \\\\ 1 & -1\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{4}[\\begin{aligned}3 \\\\ -1\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}]\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nThe acute angle between $x$ and $S$ is the acute angle between $x$ and ${\\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ Equivalently, it is the acute angle between $x$ and any non-zero vector that is parallel to ${\\text{proj}}_{S}x.$ So, to make calculations easier, we can find the angle between the vectors\n\n$\\,$ $x=[\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -1 \\\\ 1\\end{aligned}]\\,$ and $\\,2\\,{\\text{proj}}_{S}x=[\\begin{aligned}1 \\\\ 1 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}].$\n\nComputing the cosine using the dot product, we obtain\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\\operatorname{cos}⁡\\theta  & =\\frac{2\\cdot 1+(-1)\\cdot 1+1\\cdot 2}{\\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\\\  & =\\frac{3}{\\sqrt{6}\\sqrt{6}} \\\\  & =\\frac{1}{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore, \n\n$$\n\\theta =\\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\\frac{1}{2})=\\frac{\\pi }{3},\n$$\n\nwhich is already an acute angle."} {:db/id 17592186184854 :question/id #uuid "c01292af-92a2-5636-a2fa-43836bcbfa48" orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace is to find the shortest distance between the vector and the subspace.\n\nGiven a vector $\\mathbf{x}$ and a subspace $S = \\textrm{Span}\\{ \\mathbf{a}_1, \\mathbf{a}_2 \\},$ the **distance between $\\mathbf{x}$ and $S$** is given by \n\n$$\n\\Vert \\mathbf{x} - \\textrm{proj}_{S}\\mathbf{x} \\Vert\n$$\n\nas shown in the diagram below.\n\n![](images/d1/d10fd1778529183deb6912cebe9d2b7ad405091fe21a261c464d3d22c6d0860b.png)\n\nLet's find the distance between the vector $\\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace spanned by the linearly independent vectors $\\{\\mathbf{a}_1,\\mathbf{a}_2 \\},$ where\n\n![](images/83/83f52159171e736c7ee9edbd0593442d2282572db667eca483e5a77d0b73c9f7.svg)\n\nThe orthogonal projection of $\\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\textrm{proj}_{S} \\: \\mathbf{x} = A(A^T\\!A)^{-1}\\!A^T\\,\\mathbf{x}.\n$$\n\nIn this case, we have \n![](images/9e/9eca38b4b340e44108b073e3f939ce29ae96345b9c1870b9e2cc57a98f9cb077.svg)\nTherefore, we get the following projection: \n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}{\\text{proj}}_{S}\\,x & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ -1 & -2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot {([\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\\\ 2 & -1 & -2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ -1 & -2\\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\\\ 2 & -1 & -2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}0 \\\\ 2 \\\\ 4\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ -1 & -2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot {[\\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\\\ 4 & 9\\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}-4 \\\\ -10\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ -1 & -2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot \\frac{1}{2}[\\begin{aligned}9 & -4 \\\\ -4 & 2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}-4 \\\\ -10\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\\\ 0 & -1 \\\\ -1 & -2\\end{aligned}]\\cdot [\\begin{aligned}2 \\\\ -2\\end{aligned}] \\\\  & =[\\begin{aligned}-2 \\\\ 2 \\\\ 2\\end{aligned}]=\\overset{^}{x}\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n \n\nFinally, using the distance formula, the distance between $\\mathbf{x}$ and the subspace $S$ is given by\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}d(x,\\overset{^}{x}) & =‖x-\\overset{^}{x}‖ \\\\  & =\\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{(0-(-2))^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2}} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{4+0+4} \\\\  & =\\sqrt{8} \\\\  & =2\\sqrt{2}.\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\n**Note:** Recall that the vector $\\textbf{x}-\\textrm{proj}_{S}\\,\\mathbf{x},$ whose norm $\\| \\textbf{x}-\\textrm{proj}_{S}\\,\\mathbf{x} \\|$ represents the distance from $\\mathbf{x}$ to $S,$ is sometimes called the **vector rejection of $\\mathbf{x}$ from $S.$**" :tutorial/id #uuid "97ecd7fd-ac4d-5cca-86c7-db064dd69609" Since the sum of the exterior angles of a triangle is $360^{\\circ}$, we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n120^{∘} + 100^{∘} + z &= 360^{∘} \\\\\n220^{∘} + z &= 360^{∘} \\\\\nz &= 140^{∘}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nNow, we can find the value of the missing interior angle at $C$:\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nm∠C &= 180^{∘} - z \\\\\n&= 180^{∘} - 140^{∘} \\\\\n&= 40^{∘}\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nTherefore,\n\n$$\nm\\angle C = 40^\\circ\n$$"} {:db/id 17592186110942 :question/id #uuid "36704eb6-c160-5e79-926b-d62d21c8555e" :question/math-academy-id "q-20682"} {:db/id 17592186111265 :question/id #uuid "ccc1bfa0-4c29-5e73-a0dd-19c004fb842c" :question/math-academy-id "q-53050"} {:db/id 17592186048534} {:db/id 17592186050477} {:db/id 17592186050650} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186111756} :activity/id #uuid "13671180-c23c-5b99-86c7-3b830ac09165" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048201 :topic/id #uuid "87ab6c72-c0cd-50e6-96db-1aee2ca30ad9" :topic/math-academy-id 1458} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186111756 :step/content {:db/id 17592186111843 :tutorial/content "Consider the following triangle, where the side $\\overline{AC}$ has been extended beyond the vertex $C$.\n\n![](images/6b/6be676cc487d17815701f3783e9eca71d7491a0e63d7ae9016fb65ad801e61d6.png)\n\nThe resulting angle $\\angle{BCD}$ is called the **exterior angle** at vertex $C$.\n\nExterior angles have the following properties:\n\n- An exterior angle and its corresponding interior angle form a linear pair and are therefore supplementary. Here, we have\n$\\underbrace{\\color{YellowOrange}m\\angle{BCD}}_{\\large\\text{Exterior}} \\:+\\: \\underbrace{\\color{blue}m\\angle{ACB}}_{\\large\\text{Interior}} = 180^\\circ$\n- The measure of an exterior angle is equal to the sum of the measures of the two non-adjacent interior angles. This is called the **exterior angles theorem**. To see why it is true, notice that since the internal angles of a triangle sum to $180^\\circ$, we have\n$m∠A + m∠B + m∠C|= 180^{∘}; m∠A + m∠C|= 180^{∘} - m∠B_(⏟)_(Exterior angle at [math]B[/math])$.\n- At each vertex of a triangle, there are two exterior angles. Then we have\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nx + y + z &= (m∠B + m∠C) + (m∠A + m∠C) + (m∠A + m∠B) \\\\\n&= 2m∠A + 2m∠B + 2m∠C \\\\\n&= 2(m∠A + m∠B + m∠C) \\\\\n&= 2(180^{∘}) \\\\\n&= Therefore, we can write the domain of this function as\n\n$$\nx\\in (-\\infty,\\infty)\n$$\n\nLet's compare this to the function\n\n$$\ng(x) = \\dfrac 1 x\n$$\n\nshown below:\n\n![](images/84/84fefed3d54e57467ca3ebcf823c6bbf5c3c6aacce2f7542230b1abacfd97f46.png)\n\nWe cannot substitute the value $x=0$ into the function $g(x)$ because division by zero is undefined. Therefore, the domain of $g(x)$ is\n\n$$\nx\\in (-\\infty, 0)\\cup (0,\\infty)\n$$\n\nThis notation means that any number *apart from zero* can be used as an input for $g(x)$." :tutorial/id #uuid The function has critical points at $x=-1$, $x=2$, and an inflection point at $x=0.5$.\nHow can we sketch the graph of the derivative $f'(x)$?\n\n![](images/b3/b3fcc7a08d2a083567cc2de62c9bb0c6e9516552c8a2f08d2e814604f5ec84f8.png)\n\nNotice the following:\n\n- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have $f'(x)=0$.\n- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $f'(x) > 0$.\n- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have $f'(x) < 0$.\n\nWe can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below:\n\n| $x$ | $(-\\infty,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\\infty)$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $f$ | $\\nearrow$ | $\\textrm{max}$ | $\\searrow$ | $\\textrm{min}$ | $\\nearrow$ |\n| $f'$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |\n\nUsing this information, we can identify the regions where $f'(x)$ should cross the $x$-axis. According to the table, these are points $(-1,0)$ and $(2,0)$:\n\n![](images/e9/e98d21084e06d2a28509b0b68f449c5f42959ee1adad9b3dbf912885968a3b33.png)\n\nAdditionally, we are told that the function has an inflection point at $x = 0.5$. So $f''(0.5)=0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y=f'(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.\n\nWe don't know the exact value of $f'(0.5)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x)$, we can conclude that at $x = 0.5$ the slope is negative. Therefore, we get a point below the $x$-axis:\n\n![](images/59/5994a9139fbd1c530692a2fb40b2fb1b4b7bd0b34b2bf7ff7194390542748977.png)\n\nFinally, connecting up the parts of the graph above, we get an approximate sketch of $f'(x)$:\n\n![](images/f2/f21fca7744d7196e457f0a9d4511f644a3cf1e8c61018c152fc74ea7f6999f3e.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "732e85fe-aec5-51f6-806c-68e476077346" The function has critical points at $x=-1$, $x=2$, and an inflection point at $x=0.5$.\nHow can we sketch the graph of the derivative $f'(x)$?\n\n![](images/b3/b3fcc7a08d2a083567cc2de62c9bb0c6e9516552c8a2f08d2e814604f5ec84f8.png)\n\nNotice the following:\n\n- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have $f'(x)=0$.\n- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have $f'(x) > 0$.\n- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have $f'(x) < 0$.\n\nWe can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below:\n\n| $x$ | $(-\\infty,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,2)$ | $2$ | $(2,\\infty)$ |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| $f$ | $\\nearrow$ | $\\textrm{max}$ | $\\searrow$ | $\\textrm{min}$ | $\\nearrow$ |\n| $f'$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |\n\nUsing this information, we can identify the regions where $f'(x)$ should cross the $x$-axis. According to the table, these are points $(-1,0)$ and $(2,0)$:\n\n![](images/e9/e98d21084e06d2a28509b0b68f449c5f42959ee1adad9b3dbf912885968a3b33.png)\n\nAdditionally, we are told that the function has an inflection point at $x = 0.5$. So $f''(0.5)=0$ and the tangent to the graph of $y=f'(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis.\n\nWe don't know the exact value of $f'(0.5)$ but from the graph of $y=f(x)$, we can conclude that at $x = 0.5$ the slope is negative. 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1007 "Mathematics for Machine Learning" 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1008 "Our Mathematics for Machine Learning course provides a comprehensive foundation of the essential mathematical tools required to study modern machine learning.\nThis course is divided into three main categories: linear algebra, multivariable calculus, and probability & statistics. The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.\nOn completing this course, students will be well-prepared for a university-level machine learning course that tackles concepts such as gradient descent, neural networks, backpropagation, support vector machines, naive Bayes classifiers, and Gaussian mixture models." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics in set theory and logic. Students develop a precise mathematical language for describing sets, functions, and predicates, and are introduced to key ideas such as supremum and infimum, as well as argmax and argmin notation. Logical reasoning and Boolean functions are also studied, providing important conceptual motivation for understanding the expressive limitations of some simple machine learning models, such as why certain functions (e.g. XOR) cannot be represented by a single-layer neural network.\nStudents then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.\nAs part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.\nStudents will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.\nThe course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.\nA solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.\nStudents also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.\nStudents work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.\nOn the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.\nStudents extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.\nThe course concludes with parametric inference, focusing on point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals, which form the statistical foundation for many machine learning methods." 17592186045417] [17592186046658 1012 145 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.\nStudents learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.\nStudents then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.\nThe course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.\nThe course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.\nStudents then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.\nThe final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating Students will extend and formalize their understanding of sets and learn to translate between logical and set operations. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how set theory provides a comprehensive toolkit for proving mathematical results.\nAfter mastering these fundamentals, students will explore various proof-writing techniques, including direct proof, proof by cases, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, disproof, and mathematical induction. The course emphasizes proving concepts related to parity, divisibility, congruence, sequences, functions, set identities, and relations. Students will have multiple opportunities to test and refine their proof construction and comprehension skills throughout the course and in varied contexts\nThis challenging yet engaging course helps \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)} & < p < p^(^) + 1.96 \\cdot \\sqrt{(p^(^)(1 - p^(^)))/(n)}\\end{bmatrix}\n$$\n\nTherefore, a $95\\%$ confidence interval for the population proportion ${p}$ is given
